title: Haloalkanes
keyIdea: A haloalkane is an alkane with a halogen atom in place of a hydrogen, named with a prefix and a position number, as in 2-bromopropane. The C–X bond is polar, so nucleophiles such as OH⁻ and NH₃ attack the δ+ carbon and replace the halogen. The weaker the C–X bond, the faster this happens: iodo > bromo > chloro. In CFCs, UV breaks the weaker C–Cl bond, and each Cl• radical frees itself again and again to destroy ozone, which is why CFCs were banned.

kid: Take an alkane and swap one H for a halogen atom. You get a haloalkane. Its name has a prefix for the halogen: fluoro, chloro, bromo or iodo. A number says which carbon it is on. Count from the end that gives the smaller number. So CH₃CHBrCH₃ is 2-bromopropane.

The halogen pulls the shared electrons in the C–X bond towards itself. That leaves the carbon slightly positive, δ+. A nucleophile is a particle with a lone pair, such as OH⁻ or NH₃. It attacks the δ+ carbon, and the halide ion leaves. With warm NaOH, bromoethane turns into ethanol. With ammonia, it turns into ethylamine.

Which haloalkane reacts fastest? You might guess the one with the most polar bond. But the C–X bond has to break, so the weakest bond wins. C–I is the weakest, then C–Br, then C–Cl. With silver nitrate, an iodoalkane gives a yellow solid first, a bromoalkane a cream one next, and a chloroalkane a white one last.

CFCs, such as CCl₂F₂, are haloalkanes with chlorine and fluorine. They do not burn and are not toxic, so they were used in fridges and spray cans. But they are so stable that they last long enough to reach the ozone layer. There, UV light breaks a C–Cl bond and frees a Cl• radical. One Cl• destroys an O₃, then gets free again, over and over. That is why CFCs were banned.
adult: This topic, for ages 16 to 18, covers naming haloalkanes, their nucleophilic substitution reactions and the chemistry behind the ban on CFCs. Names follow IUPAC rules: a prefix for each halogen (fluoro, chloro, bromo, iodo), the lowest position numbers, and prefixes in alphabetical order when there are several, as in 1-bromo-2-chloroethane.

Halogens are more electronegative than carbon, so the C–X bond is polar with a δ+ carbon. A nucleophile donates a lone pair to that carbon and the halide leaves. Warm aqueous OH⁻ gives an alcohol, and excess ammonia in ethanol, heated in a sealed tube, gives a primary amine. Hot OH⁻ in ethanol instead favours elimination to an alkene.

Rate is set by bond enthalpy, not polarity. Typical mean values are C–F 467, C–Cl 346, C–Br 290 and C–I 228 kJ/mol, and sources vary a little. Warming each haloalkane with aqueous silver nitrate in ethanol shows the order: AgI (yellow) forms first, then AgBr (cream), then AgCl (white).

In the stratosphere, UV breaks C–Cl, not the stronger C–F, giving Cl•. Then Cl• + O₃ → ClO• + O₂ and ClO• + O₃ → Cl• + 2O₂, so the net change is 2O₃ → 3O₂ with Cl• as a catalyst. The Montreal Protocol (1987) phased CFCs out. Common mistakes: numbering from the wrong end, saying polarity sets the rate, thinking Cl• is used up, and linking the ozone hole to global warming.

familyTip: Look at the label on an old fridge or an aerosol can and see what gas it uses. Then ask: why would a gas that is safe in a kitchen be a problem 20 km up? The answer is the C–Cl bond and UV light.

practice.hint: Count the carbons, then number from the end nearer the Br.
practice.explain: Three carbons gives propane. The Br is on carbon 1 from the nearer end, so it is 1-bromopropane.

practice.prompt: A straight-chain haloalkane has {n} carbons and one Cl atom. How many hydrogen atoms does it have?
practice.hint: The alkane has 2n + 2 hydrogens. The Cl takes the place of one.
practice.explain: The alkane has 2 × {n} + 2 hydrogens; one is replaced by Cl, leaving {=2*n+1}.

practice.prompt: Warm aqueous NaOH reacts with 1-bromobutane. What attacks, and what forms?
choices: OH⁻ attacks the δ+ carbon; butan-1-ol forms
Na⁺ attacks the bromine; sodium butane forms
OH⁻ attacks the bromine; bromobutanol forms
practice.hint: The nucleophile has a lone pair and a negative charge.
practice.explain: OH⁻ is the nucleophile. It bonds to the δ+ carbon, Br⁻ leaves, and the product is the alcohol butan-1-ol.

practice.prompt: One Cl• goes round the ozone cycle {k} times. Each cycle destroys 2 O₃. How many O₃ molecules does it destroy?
practice.hint: Cl• + O₃ → ClO• + O₂, then ClO• + O₃ → Cl• + 2O₂. Count the O₃ in one lap.
practice.explain: Each lap uses 2 O₃ and gives back the Cl•, so {k} laps destroy 2 × {k} = {=2*k} O₃.

practice.prompt: Which order shows the fastest reaction with silver nitrate first?
choices: They all react at the same rate
practice.hint: The C–X bond has to break. Which one is weakest?
practice.explain: C–I (228 kJ/mol) is weakest, then C–Br (290), then C–Cl (346), so iodo reacts first and chloro last.

pool.hint: Four carbons. Which end is nearer the Br?
pool.explain: Four carbons is butane. Counting from the left end, Br is on carbon 2, which is lower than 3, so it is 2-bromobutane.

pool.prompt: Why does a nucleophile attack the carbon in a C–Cl bond?
choices: Cl pulls the bond electrons, so the carbon is δ+
The carbon is δ− and attracts it
The chlorine has no electrons left
pool.hint: Which atom is more electronegative, C or Cl?
pool.explain: Chlorine is more electronegative, so the C–Cl bond is polar with a δ+ carbon that attracts the lone pair of a nucleophile.

pool.prompt: Bond enthalpies: C–Cl 346 kJ/mol and C–I 228 kJ/mol. How much more energy is needed to break {n} mol of C–Cl bonds than {n} mol of C–I bonds, in kJ?
pool.hint: Find the difference for 1 mol, then multiply.
pool.explain: 346 − 228 = 118 kJ per mol, so for {n} mol it is 118 × {n} = {=118*n} kJ.

pool.prompt: In the silver nitrate test, which haloalkane gives a cream precipitate?
pool.hint: AgCl is white and AgI is yellow.
pool.explain: AgBr is cream. It forms after the yellow AgI but before the white AgCl.

pool.prompt: Why does UV break C–Cl rather than C–F in CCl₂F₂?
choices: C–Cl is a much weaker bond
C–F is not a covalent bond
Fluorine has no electrons to give
pool.hint: Compare the bond enthalpies: 346 and 467 kJ/mol.
pool.explain: C–Cl (346 kJ/mol) is weaker than C–F (467 kJ/mol), so stratospheric UV breaks C–Cl and releases Cl•.

pool.prompt: A haloalkane CₙH₂ₙ₊₁Br has n = {n}. Find its relative formula mass. (C = 12, H = 1, Br = 80)
pool.hint: Count C, H and Br atoms, then add their masses.

pool.prompt: Bromoethane is heated with excess ammonia in ethanol in a sealed tube. What is the main organic product?
pool.hint: NH₃ is the nucleophile here. What group replaces Br?
pool.explain: NH₃ replaces Br, then loses H⁺, giving the amine CH₃CH₂NH₂; excess ammonia mops up the HBr as NH₄Br.

pool.prompt: What is the role of Cl• in the destruction of ozone?
choices: A catalyst: it is regenerated after each cycle
A reactant that is used up by one O₃
A greenhouse gas that warms the ozone
pool.hint: Look at what comes out of the second step: ClO• + O₃ → ?
pool.explain: ClO• + O₃ → Cl• + 2O₂ gives back Cl•, so it is a catalyst and can destroy many thousands of O₃.

pool.prompt: Why were CFCs once used in fridges and spray cans?
choices: They are unreactive, non-toxic and non-flammable
pool.hint: Think about what makes a gas safe to use at home.
pool.explain: CFCs are very stable, not toxic and do not burn. That same stability lets them survive to reach the stratosphere.

visual.caption: Sort each haloalkane by the number its name needs.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: name haloalkanes, swap the halogen, race them with silver nitrate, then chase a CFC's Cl• through ozone.
